Release and Deprecation Policy

Jonathan Payne, Environment Agency Flood Forecasting

November 2026

Source: vignettes/release_policy.Rmd
release_policy.Rmd

Audience: technical. You maintain the package, depend on it from other code, or review a change to it.

Status

This is a proposal, written by the package’s author, for its owner to accept or change. It records how changes have been handled so far and what the author would hold to from here. Nothing in it has been agreed by the Environment Agency. Release D covers the governance questions that need an owner: who may release, who reviews, and where the package may run. They are listed at the end.

What this policy is for

A rating is a record that may be reviewed years after it was fitted. A change to the package must not quietly change what an old rating means, and a user should never learn about a change by finding that their code stopped working. Three rules follow.

  1. Say it. Every change a user could notice is in NEWS.md, and a change that alters behaviour or numbers is marked as such.
  2. Warn before removing. Nothing is removed without first being documented as superseded and then warning, each for at least one release.
  3. Never load what is not understood. A stored rating from a layout the package does not understand is refused with a reason, not loaded half-read.

Versions

The package is below 1.0, so the version is 0.minor.patch.

Change Bumps
A bug fix, a documentation change, a new function that changes nothing existing patch
A new feature, a deprecation, or a breaking change minor
The first release the owner declares fit for live forecasting, after the Release D gate 1.0.0

Below 1.0, a minor release may break things. That is allowed only if NEWS.md says so under the entry, in words a user would find. From 1.0, a breaking change waits for a major version.

What counts as breaking

A change is breaking if code or a stored rating that worked before may not work, or may give a different answer, after it.

  • An exported function’s name, arguments, argument defaults, or the shape of what it returns: its columns, their names, their order, their types.
  • A default that changes a result. Example: apply_rating() on a rating from fit_rating() used to refuse stages beyond the gauged range, and now returns them flagged. That was a behaviour change and NEWS.md says so.
  • The numbers. A change to the mathematics, or to a threshold’s default, that moves a result by more than rounding. It is flagged as a mathematical change, and vignette("mathematical_contract") is updated in the same change.
  • The stored layout of a rating object. See schema versions below.

These are not breaking, and may change in any release: anything whose name starts with a dot, the exact wording of a message or a printed summary, and the appearance of a plot. Test for a message’s meaning, not its words.

Deprecation

A function, argument or column goes through three stages. Each stage lasts at least one minor release.

Stage What happens What the user sees
1. Superseded The replacement exists. The old one is documented as superseded, with its replacement named, and keeps working exactly as before. The help page and NEWS.md
2. Deprecated The old one still works but warns, once per call, naming the replacement. A warning in the console
3. Removed It is gone. The removal is in NEWS.md. An error: the function does not exist

A function is never removed straight from stage 1, and a warning is never added in the same release that announces the replacement, except for a function that was already wrong.

The register

What is in the stages now. A test keeps this table in step with the “Deprecated” group in the package’s reference index.

Function Stage Replacement
rating_plot() 1. Superseded autoplot()
suggested_breakpoints_vector() 2. Deprecated the selected column of suggest_breakpoints()
bootstrap_to_table() 2. Deprecated rating_bootstrap()

rating_plot() is held at stage 1 on purpose. It is used in several vignettes and the walkthrough script, and a warning now would flood every page. The vignettes move to autoplot() first, and then it warns.

fit <- fit_rating(
  data.frame(stage_m = seq(0.3, 3, length.out = 20),
             discharge_cms = 3 * seq(0.3, 3, length.out = 20)^1.6),
  quiet = TRUE
)
w <- tryCatch(bootstrap_to_table(fit), warning = function(w) conditionMessage(w))
cat(strwrap(w, 78), sep = "\n")
#> bootstrap_to_table() is deprecated and will be removed in a later release.
#> Use rating_bootstrap(), which gives the same draws with lower_stage_m and
#> upper_stage_m in place of lower_level and upper_level.

Schema versions

Every rating object carries a schema_version, the layout it was made under. It is bumped when, and only when, the stored layout changes: a property added, removed, renamed or given a different meaning.

When it is bumped:

  1. The release must carry a migration from the previous version, or say in NEWS.md that none exists and why.
  2. A migration is a function from one version to the next, tested on an object saved under the old layout. They chain: version 2 to 3 to 4.
  3. A rating from a version with no migration is refused with the reason, and a rating from a newer version than the package knows is refused and told to update the package. Neither is loaded and guessed at.

There are no migrations yet. Version 2 is the first that carries a version, so the mechanism in import_rating() is in place and tested, with nothing to run.

rating_schema_version()
#> [1] 2

Releasing

A release is made only when all of these hold. They are what the continuous integration checks, plus what no machine can check.

  1. The full test suite passes. A new function has tests, and a fix has a test that fails without it.
  2. R CMD check has no errors and no warnings on Linux and Windows, on the current and the previous R release. The compiled core is also built and tested with gcc and clang on Linux and with clang on macOS, but the full package check is not run on macOS. Notes are read, not ignored.
  3. Every example runs, and every vignette builds.
  4. check_man() and the reference index are clean, and every exported function is in the index.
  5. NEWS.md has an entry for every change a user could notice, with breaking and mathematical changes marked.
  6. The deprecation register above matches the code.
  7. The version is bumped as the table says.
  8. A person who did not write the change has looked at it.

The last item is the one a machine cannot do. Passing checks do not stand in for a review.

What the owner needs to decide

These are not mine to decide, and the policy does not pretend otherwise.

  • Who may release, and who reviews a change before it does. Item 8 above needs a named person.
  • How long a stage lasts. One minor release is the least the policy says. If users run the package on a slow upgrade cycle, it should be longer, and the owner knows the cycle.
  • Where the package is distributed. Today it is installed from GitHub. If it is to go to an internal repository, the release steps change.
  • When 1.0.0 is. The package is classed Tier 3 in its source headers, and the Release D gate must be met before live forecasting use. That gate is mostly documents: ownership, a dependency inventory, a limitations register, a runbook, fallback and rollback, handover, a test on the target machines, and an independent review.
